Cross-modality Person Re-identification¶

COMP9444 Group Project · Group "KeyError: 'GroupName'" · Visible–infrared retrieval on SYSU-MM01

We study infrared-to-visible person retrieval with the Progressive Modality-shared Transformer (PMT) as the baseline. We test two extensions of our own design, a smooth grey-to-colour transition (S) and auxiliary local supervision (L), and channel augmentation (CA) taken from CAJ [4]. All are compared under one data split, sampler and evaluator. The final stage retrains PMT and the candidate chosen on validation (PMT + CA) on 395 identities and evaluates them once on the test split.

How to run this notebook. All results are loaded from measurements embedded in the cells below, so Restart & Run All needs no dataset, GPU or checkpoint and reproduces every table and figure. The full code is in project_code.zip, submitted with this notebook (Appendix A); training and evaluation need the dataset and an NVIDIA GPU.

Summary of findings¶

  • Baselines (validation, three seeds). PMT (M0) reaches 34.6 mAP / 32.2 Rank-1. It is above a plain ViT (V0) and the CNN baseline AGW on all 30 seed–gallery pairs, and 0.8 mAP above our corrected CAJ (CAJfix). CAJ with the authors' code collapsed during training; a one-line correction restored it (Section 5.3).
  • Extensions. S gives 34.35 ± 0.56 mAP versus M0’s 34.57 ± 0.46 across three seeds; it shows no demonstrated retrieval benefit (Section 5.4). Local supervision gives 34.7 mAP / 32.0 Rank-1 for M2* versus M0’s 34.6 / 32.2 across three seeds; optional local-feature fusion changes retrieval and is evaluated separately (Section 5.5). Band erasing (M0 + BE, M2* + BE), our own augmentation, reduces clean mAP by 0.9–1.0 and is lower under eight of nine perturbations, so it was dropped (Section 5.5).
  • Channel augmentation. PMT + CA (M0 + CA) is the only configuration clearly above M0 on validation: 36.0 vs 34.6 mAP (+1.45), higher on all three seeds and 28 of 30 seed–gallery pairs. It was therefore taken to the final stage.
  • Final test. Retrained on all 395 training identities and evaluated once on the test set, M0 reaches 64.6 mAP / 66.3 Rank-1 in All-search, within 0.4 mAP of the published PMT result. M0 + CA reaches 66.2 / 68.2 (+1.6 mAP, higher on every seed and on 28 of 30 seed–gallery pairs) and 78.4 mAP in Indoor-search (+1.55, 30 of 30). The gain holds under all nine perturbations and on the 224 naturally occluded queries (Section 5.7).

1. Introduction, Motivation and Problem Statement¶

Visible–infrared person re-identification matches an infrared query image to visible-light images of the same person across cameras. Differences in spectrum, lighting, pose and occlusion make appearance matching difficult. The objective is to learn features that preserve identity across modalities and rank matching gallery images highly, including for identities unseen during training.

We use the Progressive Modality-shared Transformer (PMT) [1] as our baseline. We investigate whether a smoother grey-to-colour transition and auxiliary local supervision improve retrieval, individually and together, and whether channel augmentation from a CNN method transfers to PMT. Performance is assessed with mAP, mINP and Rank-1/5/10/20 on identity-disjoint evaluation data.

Research questions:

  • RQ1. Does a smooth greyscale transition improve retrieval and stability around the stage switch, compared with PMT's direct switch?
  • RQ2. Can local patch-feature supervision complement the global feature, especially when part of the body is missing?
  • RQ3. Are the two extensions complementary, and is any gain worth its extra cost?

[TODO — All members (integration)] Check the motivation paragraph against the final results; add one sentence on how open-set retrieval differs from closed-set classification.

2. Data Sources¶

We use SYSU-MM01 [2] with its official identity splits. Cameras 1, 2, 4 and 5 capture RGB images; cameras 3 and 6 capture infrared images.

The dataset contains 45,863 images: 30,071 RGB and 15,792 IR. Development uses 296 training identities and 99 validation identities; 96 test identities are reserved for final evaluation. The downloaded directories contain 22 additional identities absent from the official split lists. Their 1,118 images are excluded.

Data manifest and label maps. The dataset is used as distributed: six folders cam1–cam6, each with one sub-folder per identity, plus the official lists exp/train_id.txt, val_id.txt and test_id.txt. src/data.py scans every image once and writes a manifest with one row per image: relative path, identity, camera, modality, split, image size, SHA-256, whether it decodes, and intensity statistics. All later steps (sampler, evaluation sets, the EDA below) read this manifest, and its SHA-256 is recorded with each run, so every member trains and evaluates on exactly the same files. scripts/prepare_data.py builds the manifest and the audit (Section 3.2, E5) with one command and stops if an audit check fails.

The 22 unlisted identities were found by comparing the identity folders on disk (513 identities, IDs up to 533) with the union of the three official lists (491 identities). They hold 1,118 images; 19 of them have RGB images only and 3 IR images only, so most could not be used for cross-modality training anyway. They are marked unassigned in the manifest and never read.

Training labels are built by build_label_map: identities of the training split(s) that have both RGB and IR images, sorted by identity number and numbered 0 … C − 1. Development uses the training split (296 classes); the final stage uses training + validation (395 classes). Validation and test identities keep their original numbers and are used only for retrieval, never as classes.

In [ ]:
# Excerpt of src/data.py: the label maps and the 2PK batch plan of PMTBatchSampler (image loading and augmentation omitted).
from collections import defaultdict

SAMPLER_STREAM = 101    # separate random stream from augmentation, so changing the grey probability never changes the images drawn


def build_label_map(rows, train_splits=("train",)):
    """Identity -> class 0 .. C-1, sorted by identity; only identities with both RGB and IR images.
    Development: ("train",) gives 296 classes; final stage: ("train", "val") gives 395."""
    has = defaultdict(set)
    for r in rows:
        if r["split"] in train_splits and r["decode_ok"]:
            has[r["identity"]].add(r["modality"])
    eligible = sorted(pid for pid, mods in has.items() if mods == {"rgb", "ir"})
    return {pid: label for label, pid in enumerate(eligible)}


def epoch_plan(rows, label_map, P=8, K=4, seed=17, epoch=0):
    """One epoch of 2PK batches; depends only on (seed, epoch), so runs can be resumed and reproduced.
    Each batch: P distinct identities, K RGB rows per identity, then the same identities' K IR rows in the same order.
    An identity with fewer than K images of a modality is drawn with replacement (never needed on SYSU-MM01, see E2)."""
    pos = {"rgb": defaultdict(list), "ir": defaultdict(list)}
    for i, r in enumerate(rows):
        if r["identity"] in label_map and r["decode_ok"]:
            pos[r["modality"]][r["identity"]].append(i)
    identities = sorted(label_map)
    steps = max(sum(map(len, pos["rgb"].values())), sum(map(len, pos["ir"].values()))) // (P * K)
    rng = np.random.default_rng([seed, SAMPLER_STREAM, epoch])
    plan = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        pids = [identities[j] for j in rng.choice(len(identities), P, replace=False)]
        rgb, ir = [], []
        for pid in pids:
            for half, modality in ((rgb, "rgb"), (ir, "ir")):
                pool = pos[modality][pid]
                half += [pool[j] for j in rng.choice(len(pool), K, replace=len(pool) < K)]
        plan.append(rgb + ir)
    return plan

# Check on a synthetic manifest: 6 training identities (one without IR images) and 3 validation identities.
synthetic = [{"identity": pid, "split": split, "modality": m, "decode_ok": True}
             for pid, split in [(1, "train"), (2, "train"), (3, "train"), (5, "train"), (8, "train"), (9, "train"),
                                (11, "val"), (12, "val"), (13, "val")]
             for m in ("rgb", "ir") if not (pid == 9 and m == "ir")
             for _ in range(6 if m == "rgb" else 3)]
dev_map, final_map = build_label_map(synthetic), build_label_map(synthetic, ("train", "val"))
plan = epoch_plan(synthetic, dev_map, P=4, K=2, seed=17)
layout_ok = all(
    [synthetic[i]["identity"] for i in b[:8]] == [synthetic[i]["identity"] for i in b[8:]]        # same identities, RGB then IR
    and all(synthetic[i]["modality"] == "rgb" for i in b[:8]) and all(synthetic[i]["modality"] == "ir" for i in b[8:])

    and all(synthetic[b[j]]["identity"] == synthetic[b[j + 1]]["identity"] for j in range(0, 16, 2))  # K consecutive rows
    for b in plan)

3. Exploratory Analysis of Data¶

3.1 Data balance and integrity¶

The training split has 20,284 RGB images and 9,929 IR images, approximately a 2:1 imbalance. We therefore sample equally from both modalities and balance identities within each training batch. All training identities have images in both modalities. The audit found no unreadable images, overlapping official identity splits or duplicate files shared across splits.

Camera-level image counts also vary, as shown below. These counts describe dataset coverage; they do not establish how difficult each camera is for retrieval.

E1 — Data composition. Observation: the training split has 20,284 RGB and 9,929 IR images (about 2 : 1) from all six cameras. The validation identities appear in only three cameras: all 1,980 validation IR images come from the indoor camera 3, and the RGB gallery from cameras 4 and 5. The test split covers all six cameras, with 1,883 IR queries from camera 3 and 1,920 from the outdoor camera 6. Impact: a sampler that draws images uniformly would give IR only a third of each batch; and validation measures indoor IR → RGB retrieval only, so problems specific to camera 6 cannot appear there. Decision: every batch holds the same identities with equally many RGB and IR images (Section 3.3); model selection uses validation with this limitation stated (Section 6.3), and camera-6 behaviour is described only once, on the test set (natural-occlusion subset below, error analysis in Section 5.8).

E2 — Identity coverage. Observation: IR counts per training identity are nearly fixed (20 per IR camera: 96 identities have 20, the rest 40–46), while RGB counts range from 10 to 144 (median 87). Every training identity has at least 10 RGB and 20 IR images, and 180 of the 296 appear in all six cameras. Impact: sampling images uniformly would let identities with many RGB images dominate the identity and triplet losses; on the other hand, every identity has enough images for K = 4 per modality without repeats. Decision: the sampler first draws P identities uniformly, then K images per identity and modality (PMT's 2PK layout). With P = 8, K = 4 no draw needs replacement, and every identity is seen 7–30 times per epoch (seed 17).

E3 — Image quality. Observation: crops differ widely in size (median height 269 px for RGB and 306 px for IR; 5th–95th percentile about 140–470 px), and most are narrower than the 2 : 1 model input (median height/width 2.66 RGB, 2.82 IR). IR images are brighter (median 119 vs 95) and lower in contrast (pixel SD 37 vs 47). The IR cameras store the same value in all three channels (channel spread 0 for 97–99% of images), whereas RGB cameras have a median spread of 7–10. We did not measure sharpness. Impact: resizing to 256 × 128 slightly widens most people, equally for all models; colour, the strongest cue between RGB images, does not exist on the IR side. Decision: one fixed resize and ImageNet normalisation for every model (Section 4.6); RGB images are converted to grey in PMT's first stage so both modalities start in one colour space, and S and CA vary this step (Sections 4.3, 4.5). Blur is instead tested as a perturbation in the robustness evaluation (Sections 4.7 and 5.5).

E4 — Paired examples and occlusion. Panel (a) shows one training identity in all six cameras; panel (b) shows naturally occluded test IR queries from the subset described below.

Observation: besides colour, viewpoint, scale and background change between cameras as much as between modalities; clothing shape and texture are kept in IR. To see whether real occlusion can be studied during development, we checked all 1,980 validation IR queries one by one against a fixed rule (an object, another person or the frame edge hides about 10% or more of the body): none qualifies, because validation IR comes from one indoor corridor camera. We then applied the same rule to the 3,803 test IR queries, before any model had been evaluated on the test set, and found 224 occluded queries of 73 identities. The first pass was done with an AI assistant and every entry was then checked by hand by Member A; the list (annotations/natural_occlusion_test_ir.csv, paths and labels only) was committed to Git before the first test evaluation, and the evaluation script refuses an uncommitted list.

Both plans show the model the same share of the data (about 56% of RGB and 85% of IR training images each epoch, with no repeated draws); they differ only in batch structure. Q gives each anchor twice as many negative identities (15 vs 7) but half as many cross-modality positives (2 vs 4), which also leaves MSEL and DCL fewer images per identity centre. Any difference between Q and M0 on validation can therefore be attributed to this trade-off rather than to data exposure.

3.3 Pre-processing¶

The data properties above lead to the following processing, applied identically to every model:

  • Cleaning (E5). The 22 identities that appear in the image folders but in none of the official split lists (1,118 images) are excluded. All remaining images are readable and no file is shared between splits; the 37 byte-identical pairs lie within one identity and split and are kept.
  • Classes (Section 2, E1). Each identity is a class for the identity loss only: 296 classes in development and 395 in the final stage (train + validation). Validation and test identities are never seen in training, so evaluation is open-set retrieval rather than classification.
  • Resizing and normalisation (E3). Images are resized once at load time to 256 × 128 for the ViT models and 288 × 144 for the ResNet-50 baselines, then normalised with ImageNet statistics. Evaluation uses only this resizing and normalisation.
  • Modality and identity balance (E1, E2, Q). Because RGB images outnumber IR about 2 : 1 and RGB counts per identity vary from 10 to 144, every training batch draws identities uniformly and the same identities in both modalities: 8 identities × 4 images × 2 modalities.
  • Colour gap (E3, E4). IR images have no colour information. PMT trains its first stage on greyscale RGB, so that RGB and IR inputs first share one colour space; S, CA and band erasing modify this augmentation step (Section 4).
  • Occlusion (E4). Validation contains no natural occlusion, so development uses synthetic occlusion only; the natural-occlusion subset of the test set is reported once, descriptively (Section 5.7).

Augmentation parameters for each model are listed in Section 4.6.

4. Models and Methods¶

All models in this project share the data split, the identity-balanced sampler and the evaluator. The figure gives an overview of PMT and the optional modules; each module is switched on by configuration only, so every comparison differs from M0 in the target factor alone.

Model names used throughout: M0 = PMT; M1 = M0 + smooth transition (S), with F its fixed-probability control; M2 = M0 + local supervision (L) with q = 2 regions; M2* = M0 + L with q = 3; M3 = M0 + S + L; + CA and + BE add channel augmentation or band erasing. V0, AGW, CAJ and CAJfix (our corrected CAJ) are the comparison baselines. Configuration files for each name are listed in Appendix A.

4.1 PMT (M0)¶

PMT is the main method of this project: both proposed extensions are built on it, and it is referred to as M0 in the experiments. We implement PMT following Lu et al. [1] and the pinned author PyTorch implementation. The shared ViT-B/16 has 12 blocks, 12 attention heads and 768-dimensional features. A 16×16 patch projection with stride 12 produces a 21×10 patch grid from 256×128 images. The CLS feature feeds a BN neck and an identity classifier. Metric losses use the pre-BN feature; retrieval uses the L2-normalised, post-BN global feature.

Training has two stages. Epochs 1–6 use greyscale RGB and IR inputs with identity classification and separate within-modality hard-triplet losses. Epochs 7–24 restore colour RGB and use joint hard-triplet, modality discrepancy (MSEL) and centre-based (DCL) losses:

$$L_1=L_{ID}^{R}+L_{ID}^{I}+L_{tri}^{R}+L_{tri}^{I}.$$ $$L_2=L_{ID}^{R}+L_{ID}^{I}+L_{tri}^{all}+0.5L_{MSEL}+0.5L_{DCL}.$$

MSEL aligns within- and cross-modality positive distances; DCL encourages identity-centred separation. We retain the stage-2 ID term as in the author's PyTorch code. PMT and its losses are prior work; our contribution here is the implementation and experiment. The augmentation recipe includes the author's random-erasing implementation. Source attribution and implementation differences are recorded in ATTRIBUTION.md and docs/baseline.md.

PMT framework, from Lu et al. [1], Fig. 2. Our implementation (M0) follows it; the configuration is given in Section 4.6.

Core implementation. The cells below are excerpts of src/model.py and src/losses.py (the ViT blocks themselves are standard and omitted). Metric losses use the pre-BN CLS feature in FP32; the BN-neck output feeds the classifier and, after L2 normalisation, retrieval. A batch holds P identities × K images of RGB followed by the same identities in IR, which MSEL and DCL rely on.

In [4]:
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F


class PMT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes, model_config=None, pretrained=None):
        super().__init__()
        cfg = model_config or {}
        dim = cfg.get("global_feature_dim", 768)
        self.base = VisionTransformer(image_size=cfg.get("image_size", (256, 128)),
            patch_size=cfg.get("patch_size", 16), patch_stride=cfg.get("patch_stride", 12),
            dim=dim, depth=cfg.get("depth", 12), heads=cfg.get("heads", 12),
            dropout=cfg.get("dropout", .03), attention_dropout=cfg.get("attention_dropout", 0.),
            drop_path=cfg.get("drop_path", .1), activation_checkpointing=cfg.get("activation_checkpointing", False))
        self.bottleneck = nn.BatchNorm1d(dim)
        self.bottleneck.bias.requires_grad_(False)
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(dim, num_classes, bias=False)
        nn.init.normal_(self.classifier.weight, std=.001)
        if pretrained is not None:
            self.base.load_pretrained(pretrained)

    def forward(self, images):
        global_feature, patches, grid = self.base(images)
        bn_feature = self.bottleneck(global_feature)
        return {"global_feature": global_feature, "global_logits": self.classifier(bn_feature),
                "retrieval_feature": F.normalize(bn_feature, dim=1),
                "patch_features": patches, "patch_grid": grid,
                "local_features": None, "local_logits": None}
In [5]:
def distances(x, y):
    # FP32 even when the backbone uses autocast: avoid half-precision cancellation.
    x, y = x.float(), y.float()
    return (x.square().sum(1)[:, None] + y.square().sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * x @ y.T).clamp_min(1e-12).sqrt()


def validate_layout(labels, k):
    if k < 2 or labels.ndim != 1 or len(labels) % (2 * k):
        raise ValueError("Expected balanced 2PK labels with K >= 2")
    a, b = labels.chunk(2)
    blocks = a.reshape(-1, k)
    if (not torch.equal(a, b) or not torch.all(blocks == blocks[:, :1])
            or len(torch.unique(blocks[:, 0])) != len(blocks) or len(blocks) < 2):
        raise ValueError("Expected distinct P >= 2 identities, contiguous K samples, RGB then IR")


def hard_triplet(features, labels, margin=.1):
    d = distances(features, features)
    same = labels[:, None] == labels[None, :]
    positives = same & ~torch.eye(len(labels), dtype=torch.bool, device=labels.device)
    if not positives.any(1).all() or not (~same).any(1).all():
        raise ValueError("Triplet requires a non-self positive and a negative per anchor")
    hardest_positive = d.masked_fill(~positives, -torch.inf).max(1).values
    hardest_negative = d.masked_fill(same, torch.inf).min(1).values
    return F.relu(hardest_positive - hardest_negative + margin).mean()


def msel(features, labels, k):
    validate_layout(labels, k)
    a, b = features.chunk(2)
    target = labels[:len(a)]
    same = target[:, None] == target[None, :]
    nonself = same & ~torch.eye(len(a), dtype=torch.bool, device=labels.device)
    intra_a = (distances(a, a) * nonself).sum(1) / (k - 1)
    intra_b = (distances(b, b) * nonself).sum(1) / (k - 1)
    cross = distances(a, b)
    cross_a = (cross * same).sum(1) / k
    cross_b = (cross.T * same).sum(1) / k
    return ((cross_a - intra_a).square().mean() + (cross_b - intra_b).square().mean()) / 2


def dcl(features, labels, k):
    validate_layout(labels, k)
    identities = labels[:len(labels) // 2:k]
    same = identities[:, None] == labels[None, :]
    centers = torch.stack([features[labels == identity].mean(0) for identity in identities])
    d = distances(centers, features)
    negatives = d[~same].reshape(len(identities), -1)
    selected = (negatives < negatives.mean(1, keepdim=True)) & (negatives > 1e-6)
    # Equal distances yield no strictly-below-mean negatives in upstream code.
    # Fall back to all negatives for that center rather than returning NaN.
    selected = torch.where(selected.any(1, keepdim=True), selected, torch.ones_like(selected))
    negative_mean = ((negatives * selected).sum(1) / selected.sum(1)).mean()
    positive = d[same]
    positive = positive[positive > 1e-6]
    positive_mean = positive.mean() if positive.numel() else d.sum() * 0
    return positive_mean / negative_mean.clamp_min(1e-6)


class PMTLoss(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, k=4, margin=.1, msel_weight=.5, dcl_weight=.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.k, self.margin = k, margin
        self.msel_weight, self.dcl_weight = msel_weight, dcl_weight

    def forward(self, output, labels, stage):
        if stage not in (1, 2, "V0"):
            raise ValueError("stage must be 1, 2 or V0")
        validate_layout(labels, self.k)
        features, logits = output["global_feature"].float(), output["global_logits"].float()
        a, b = logits.chunk(2)
        la, lb = labels.chunk(2)
        identity = F.cross_entropy(a, la) + F.cross_entropy(b, lb)
        zero = features.sum() * 0
        if stage == 1:
            fa, fb = features.chunk(2)
            triplet = hard_triplet(fa, la, self.margin) + hard_triplet(fb, lb, self.margin)
        else:
            triplet = hard_triplet(features, labels, self.margin)
        modality = msel(features, labels, self.k) if stage == 2 else zero
        center = dcl(features, labels, self.k) if stage == 2 else zero
        terms = {"id": identity, "triplet": triplet, "msel": modality, "dcl": center,
                 "weighted_msel": self.msel_weight * modality, "weighted_dcl": self.dcl_weight * center}
        terms["total"] = identity + triplet + terms["weighted_msel"] + terms["weighted_dcl"]
        return terms

4.2 Comparison baselines¶

We compare M0 with three baselines trained on the same 296 identities, with the same identity-balanced sampler and evaluator, each with training seeds 17, 42 and 2026 (CAJ with the authors' code: seed 17 only).

  • V0 is M0 without PMT's components: the same ViT-B/16 trained for 24 epochs with identity and global hard-triplet losses only, without the greyscale stage, MSEL or DCL. It measures what those components add.
  • AGW [3] is a two-stream ResNet-50 with non-local blocks and GeM pooling, trained with identity and weighted regularised triplet (WRT) losses. It is a widely used CNN baseline for this task.
  • CAJ [4] extends AGW with channel augmentation (a second RGB view with one colour channel copied to all three; random channel copying or greyscale for IR) and a squared-difference triplet loss (ADP). It tests whether simple colour augmentation already gives the benefit that the smooth-transition extension targets.

AGW and CAJ were ported from the authors' code at a pinned commit [3] and keep the authors' training settings (Section 4.6). CAJ collapsed with that code; we also report a corrected CAJ, CAJfix, that changes only the hard-negative weighting (Section 5.3). The authors trained on 395 identities; we use 296 so that validation identities are never seen in training.

AGW: ResNet-50 with non-local attention, GeM pooling and the weighted regularised triplet loss, from Ye et al. [3].

CAJ: channel-augmented joint learning on original and channel-augmented images, from Ye et al. [4].

4.3 Smooth grey-to-colour transition (S: M1, control F)¶

Motivation and position in the pipeline. M0 converts every RGB training image to grayscale during epochs 1–6, then switches abruptly to colour. S tests whether a gradual return to colour eases adaptation. The added GraySchedule receives training progress and configuration and supplies a probability to RGB augmentation before the PMT encoder. RGB pixels bypass the scheduler; IR inputs, the backbone, loss-stage switching and the 768-dimensional global retrieval feature are unchanged. No learned parameters are added.

Schedule and exposure control. Let $r=t-T_1$ be the zero-based consumed-batch index after stage 1, and let $W\geq2$ be the transition window in batches. M1 uses $$p_{\mathrm{gray}}(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t<T_1,\\p_0(1-r/(W-1)),&0\leq r<W,\\0,&r\geq W.\end{cases}$$ Here $p_0=1$ and $W$ spans three epochs. Each RGB image is independently selected for grayscale conversion with probability $p$; otherwise it remains in colour. Control F uses $p_0/2=0.5$ in the same window, then zero. The probability sums are both $Wp_0/2$, so expected grayscale exposure matches for equal RGB batch sizes. Realised counts can differ. M0 uses zero immediately after stage 1. This controls expected exposure amount when testing the temporal schedule.

Relation to prior work. PBSVT [5] already investigates progressive modality transitions through staged IR, grayscale and RGB inputs and spatial mixing. S tests a different mechanism—whole-image grayscale probability within PMT—with an exposure-matched control. We do not claim to originate progressive transition training. CAJ [4] instead adds channel-based augmentation, discussed separately in Section 4.5.

Core implementation. The following 41-line excerpt is copied from src/schedules.py. The schedule is stateless: configuration and the consumed-batch index reconstruct its probability after a restart. Consumed batches include AMP-skipped optimiser updates, matching the sampler's progress. The checks below are synthetic correctness checks, not retrieval measurements.

In [16]:
"""Deterministic grayscale probabilities for the PMT transition.

Steps count consumed batches (including AMP skipped updates), as the sampler does.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
import math


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GraySchedule:
    mode: str
    stage1_steps: int
    window_steps: int
    initial_probability: float = 1.0

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.mode not in ('off', 'linear', 'fixed_expected_exposure'):
            raise ValueError('Unknown grayscale schedule mode')
        if self.stage1_steps < 0 or self.window_steps < 2:
            raise ValueError('stage1_steps must be nonnegative and window_steps >= 2')
        if not math.isfinite(self.initial_probability) or not 0 <= self.initial_probability <= 1:
            raise ValueError('initial_probability must be between 0 and 1')

    def __call__(self, global_step: int) -> float:
        if not isinstance(global_step, int) or global_step < 0:
            raise ValueError('global_step must be a nonnegative integer')
        if global_step < self.stage1_steps:
            return 1.0
        r = global_step - self.stage1_steps
        if self.mode == 'off' or r >= self.window_steps:
            return 0.0
        if self.mode == 'fixed_expected_exposure':
            return self.initial_probability / 2
        return self.initial_probability * (1 - r / (self.window_steps - 1))


def from_config(config, batches_per_epoch):
    """Build a stateless schedule from the checkpointed config and sampler size."""
    if not isinstance(batches_per_epoch, int) or batches_per_epoch < 1:
        raise ValueError('batches_per_epoch must be a positive integer')
    smooth = config['smooth']
    return GraySchedule(smooth['mode'], config['training']['stage1_epochs'] * batches_per_epoch,
                        smooth['window_epochs'] * batches_per_epoch, smooth['initial_probability'])

4.4 Local supervision (L: M2, M3, q × β variants) and band erasing¶

Local identity supervision (L). To preserve identity cues across image regions, we divide PMT's $21\times10$ patch-token grid into $q$ horizontal regions. Each region is averaged, then passed through independent batch normalisation (BN) and an identity classifier. The local objective averages their cross-entropy (CE) losses and contributes weight $\beta$ to both training stages:

$$L_{\mathrm{total}}=L_{\mathrm{PMT}}+\frac{\beta}{q}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\operatorname{CE}(\ell_j,y),$$

where $\ell_j$ contains region $j$'s identity scores and $y$ is the training identity. Gradients update the shared backbone; retrieval retains PMT's 768-dimensional global BN feature.

Local representations in MLMT [6], LAReViT [7] and PAT [8] motivate the comparison. We test $q\in\{2,3\}$ and $\beta\in\{0.5,0.25\}$. M2 uses $q=2,\beta=0.5$; M2* uses $q=3,\beta=0.5$, selected on seed-17 validation. Three regions divide the grid into seven rows each. M3 combines M2 with the smooth grey-to-colour transition (S).

The code from src/local_head.py defines the local head, loss and PMT adapter. src/train.py creates the adapter before the optimiser and adds the local loss after PMTLoss. The synthetic check verifies pooling, gradients, both training stages, global retrieval and state restoration.

In [7]:
import math
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

class LocalHead(nn.Module):
    """Pool explicit row-major [N,H*W,D] patches into disjoint height bands.

    Boundary j is floor(j*H/regions). Every row belongs to exactly one band,
    including odd heights (the default 21x10 grid splits into 10 and 11 rows).
    Returns pre-BN features [N,q,D] and identity logits [N,q,C].
    """
    def __init__(self, feature_dim, num_classes, regions=2, seed=17):
        super().__init__()
        if any(type(v) is not int or v < 1 for v in (feature_dim, num_classes, regions)):
            raise ValueError("feature_dim, num_classes and regions must be positive integers")
        self.feature_dim, self.regions = feature_dim, regions
        # CPU construction and isolated generator leave the baseline RNG untouched.
        with torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[]):
            torch.random.default_generator.manual_seed(seed)
            self.necks = nn.ModuleList([nn.BatchNorm1d(feature_dim) for _ in range(regions)])
            self.classifiers = nn.ModuleList([
                nn.Linear(feature_dim, num_classes, bias=False) for _ in range(regions)])
            for neck, classifier in zip(self.necks, self.classifiers):
                neck.bias.requires_grad_(False)
                nn.init.normal_(classifier.weight, std=.001)

    def forward(self, patches, grid):
        if len(grid) != 2 or any(type(v) is not int or v < 1 for v in grid):
            raise ValueError("grid must contain explicit positive integer H and W")
        h, w = grid
        if patches.ndim != 3 or patches.shape[1:] != (h * w, self.feature_dim):
            raise ValueError("Expected [N,H*W,feature_dim] patches without special tokens")
        if h < self.regions:
            raise ValueError("Each horizontal region needs at least one row")
        spatial = patches.reshape(patches.shape[0], h, w, self.feature_dim)
        features = torch.stack([
            spatial[:, j*h//self.regions:(j+1)*h//self.regions].mean(dim=(1, 2))
            for j in range(self.regions)], dim=1)
        logits = torch.stack([classifier(neck(features[:, j]))
                              for j, (neck, classifier) in enumerate(zip(self.necks, self.classifiers))], dim=1)
        return features, logits


def local_cross_entropy(logits, labels):
    """Mean identity CE over all samples and regions, computed in FP32."""
    if logits.ndim != 3 or labels.shape != (logits.shape[0],):
        raise ValueError("Expected logits [N,q,C] and labels [N]")
    return torch.stack([F.cross_entropy(logits[:, j].float(), labels)
                        for j in range(logits.shape[1])]).mean()
In [8]:
def add_local_loss(terms, output, labels, weight=.5):
    """Use after PMTLoss in BOTH stages; preserve the original total when off."""
    if not math.isfinite(weight) or weight < 0:
        raise ValueError("Local loss weight must be finite and nonnegative")
    result = dict(terms)
    logits = output.get("local_logits")
    if logits is None or weight == 0:
        loss = terms["total"].new_zeros(())
    else:
        loss = local_cross_entropy(logits, labels)
        result["total"] = terms["total"] + weight * loss
    result.update(local=loss, local_weighted=weight * loss)
    return result


class PMTWithLocal(nn.Module):
    """Opt-in adapter; baseline state-dict keys remain unchanged.

    Construct from the already initialized PMT BEFORE creating the optimizer.
    Disabled mode creates no head. State includes local BN buffers for resume.
    """
    def __init__(self, baseline, regions=2, enabled=True, seed=17):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = baseline.base
        self.bottleneck = baseline.bottleneck
        self.classifier = baseline.classifier
        self.local_head = (LocalHead(self.classifier.in_features,
                                    self.classifier.out_features, regions, seed)
                           if enabled else None)
        self.train(baseline.training)

    def forward(self, images):
        global_feature, patches, grid = self.base(images)
        bn_feature = self.bottleneck(global_feature)
        features, logits = ((None, None) if self.local_head is None
                            else self.local_head(patches, grid))
        return dict(global_feature=global_feature,
                    global_logits=self.classifier(bn_feature),
                    retrieval_feature=F.normalize(bn_feature, dim=1),
                    patch_features=patches, patch_grid=grid,
                    local_features=features, local_logits=logits)

# Synthetic interface and gradient checks; these do not measure retrieval performance.
# The fixture supplies the same output interface as the PMT backbone.
class DFixtureBackbone(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.project = nn.Linear(3, 8)
    def forward(self, images):
        patches = self.project(images.permute(0, 2, 3, 1)).reshape(len(images), 210, 8)
        return patches.mean(1), patches, (21, 10)

class DFixturePMT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = DFixtureBackbone()
        self.bottleneck = nn.BatchNorm1d(8)
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(8, 2, bias=False)

with torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[]):
    torch.manual_seed(17)
    d_images = torch.randn(8, 3, 21, 10)
    d_labels = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1])
    d_checks = []
    for q in (2, 3):
        baseline = DFixturePMT()
        model = PMTWithLocal(baseline, regions=q)
        output = model(d_images)
        assert output['local_features'].shape == (8, q, 8)
        assert output['local_logits'].shape == (8, q, 2)
        # Exact regional pooling on a non-square grid.
        grid = output['patch_features'].reshape(8, 21, 10, 8)
        for j in range(q):
            expected = grid[:, j*21//q:(j+1)*21//q].mean((1, 2))
            torch.testing.assert_close(output['local_features'][:, j], expected)
        # The local loss itself must reach the shared backbone and every regional classifier.
        local_cross_entropy(output['local_logits'], d_labels).backward()
        assert model.base.project.weight.grad.abs().sum() > 0
        assert all(c.weight.grad.abs().sum() > 0 for c in model.local_head.classifiers)
        for stage in (1, 2):
            model.zero_grad()
            output = model(d_images)
            terms = PMTLoss(k=2)(output, d_labels, stage)
            combined = add_local_loss(terms, output, d_labels, weight=0.5)
            torch.testing.assert_close(combined['total'], terms['total'] + combined['local_weighted'])
            assert torch.isfinite(combined['total'])
            combined['total'].backward()
            assert model.base.project.weight.grad.abs().sum() > 0
            assert add_local_loss(terms, output, d_labels, weight=0)['total'] is terms['total']
        # Identical global retrieval computation with the shared baseline modules.
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            global_feature, _, _ = baseline.base(d_images)
            expected = F.normalize(baseline.bottleneck(global_feature), dim=1)
            torch.testing.assert_close(model(d_images)['retrieval_feature'], expected)
        restored = PMTWithLocal(DFixturePMT(), regions=q).eval()
        restored.load_state_dict(model.state_dict(), strict=True)
        with torch.no_grad():
            torch.testing.assert_close(restored(d_images)['local_logits'], model(d_images)['local_logits'])
        d_checks.append([q, 'PASS', 'PASS', 'PASS', 'PASS'])
show_table(['Regions', 'Grid and pooling', 'Local gradients', 'Both stages', 'Retrieval and restore'], d_checks)

Band erasing (BE: M0 + BE, M2* + BE). Band erasing is our own augmentation. It tests whether training directly on occluded images yields the robustness that L targets, without additional heads. With probability 0.5, one of q = 3 horizontal bands of the training image is filled with the ImageNet mean over its full width. The bands use the same boundaries as the local head's regions (band j covers rows ⌊jH/q⌋ to ⌊(j+1)H/q⌋), so in M2* + BE an erased band coincides exactly with one region, which must then be identified from the remaining visible parts. BE is applied to both modalities as the last training transform. With p = 0 it draws no random numbers, so every other experiment keeps its augmentation sequence. M0 + BE and M2* + BE differ from M0 and M2* only in augmentation.band_erasing = 0.5.

The core of BandErasing in src/data.py:

In [7]:
import random

IMAGENET_MEAN = (0.485, 0.456, 0.406)


class BandErasing:
    """Erase one of `regions` full-width horizontal bands with probability p (bands match the local head)."""

    def __init__(self, p=0.5, regions=3, mean=IMAGENET_MEAN):
        self.p, self.regions, self.mean = p, regions, mean

    def band(self, height, j):
        return j * height // self.regions, (j + 1) * height // self.regions

    def __call__(self, img):                      # img: normalised tensor [3, H, W]
        if self.p == 0 or random.uniform(0, 1) >= self.p:
            return img                            # p = 0 consumes no random numbers
        j = random.randrange(self.regions)
        top, bottom = self.band(img.size()[1], j)
        for c in range(img.size()[0]):
            img[c, top:bottom, :] = self.mean[c]
        return img

4.5 Channel augmentation for PMT (M0 + CA)¶

Why. Under our protocol the corrected CAJ is 3.1 mAP above AGW on every seed (Section 5.2), and channel augmentation is its cheapest component. PMT removes colour only during its six-epoch grey stage; afterwards the model can rely on colour again, which IR images lack. Channel augmentation keeps removing colour for the whole of training, and the three channels give different grey-level views of the same clothing, closer to how IR renders it. It adds no parameters and no test-time cost. It was added after the configuration freeze on 8 November, once S and L had shown no gain, with the decision rule written before its runs: M0 + CA must exceed M0 in mean validation mAP, with the same sign on every seed (Section 4.8).

How. We reuse CAJ's two operations [4] on the normalised tensor, after PMT's random erasing:

  • ChannelExchange (RGB): with probability p = 0.5, one of R, G and B is chosen at random and copied to all three channels.
  • ChannelAdapGray (IR): with probability 3/4 one channel is copied to all three; in the remaining cases it is converted to greyscale with probability 0.5 and otherwise left unchanged. SYSU-MM01 IR images already have three identical channels, so this step changes them very little.

Our change to CAJ. CAJ adds the channel-exchanged image as an extra RGB view, which doubles the RGB part of the batch (96 instead of 64 images). PMT's MSEL and DCL pair the RGB and IR halves of a 2PK batch identity by identity, so we replace the image instead of adding a view: the batch stays 8 identities × 4 images per modality, and in expectation half of the RGB samples are exchanged, as in CAJ. p = 0.5 follows CAJ and was not tuned. M0 + CA differs from M0 only in augmentation.channel_exchange = 0.5; M2* + CA adds the same key to M2*.

The operations from src/agw.py and their use in PMTTrainTransform (src/data.py):

In [9]:
def _replicate(img, channel):
    img[:] = img[channel].clone()
    return img


def _to_gray(img):
    img[:] = 0.2989 * img[0] + 0.5870 * img[1] + 0.1140 * img[2]
    return img


class ChannelExchange:
    """CAJ ChannelExchange(gray=2): randint(0, 2) always picks one colour channel to replicate."""
    def __init__(self, gray=2):
        self.gray = gray

    def __call__(self, img):
        idx = random.randint(0, self.gray)
        return _replicate(img, idx) if idx < 3 else _to_gray(img)


class ChannelAdapGray:
    """CAJ ChannelAdapGray: 3/4 replicate one channel; otherwise greyscale with this probability."""
    def __init__(self, probability=0.5):
        self.probability = probability

    def __call__(self, img):
        idx = random.randint(0, 3)
        if idx < 3:
            return _replicate(img, idx)
        if random.uniform(0, 1) > self.probability:
            return img
        return _to_gray(img)


def channel_augment(out, modality, p=0.5):
    """From PMTTrainTransform.__call__: runs after random erasing and replaces the image (no extra view)."""
    if modality == "ir":
        return ChannelAdapGray(0.5)(out)
    if random.uniform(0, 1) < p:
        return ChannelExchange(gray=2)(out)
    return out

4.6 Preprocessing and training settings¶

Each model keeps the preprocessing and optimisation settings of its original implementation; only the data split, sampler and evaluator are shared. All images are normalised using ImageNet statistics, and evaluation uses resize and normalisation only.

Setting V0 / M0 (ViT-B/16) AGW / CAJ (ResNet-50)
Initialisation Author-linked ImageNet ViT-B/16 weights ImageNet ResNet-50 weights; last-stage stride 1
Input size 256×128 288×144
Training augmentation Horizontal flip, random erasing; IR also colour jitter or Gaussian blur Pad and random crop, horizontal flip; CAJ adds channel augmentation and random erasing (p = 0.5)
Batch 8 identities × 4 images × 2 modalities = 64 Same sampler: 64 images; CAJ 96 (two RGB views)
Training length 24 epochs; M0's first 6 in stage 1 AGW 81 epochs; CAJ 100 epochs
Optimiser AdamW; weight decay 0.0001 SGD, Nesterov momentum 0.9; weight decay 0.0005
Learning rate Base 0.0003; half rate for patch projection and transformer blocks Base 0.1; ×0.1 for the backbone
Schedule 3-epoch warmup, cosine decay; minimum LR 0.000003 10-epoch linear warmup; ×0.1 at epochs 20 and 50
Metric loss Hard triplet, margin 0.1 AGW: WRT; CAJ: ADP (both soft-margin, no fixed margin)
Precision Mixed precision Full precision

The extensions (S, L, CA, band erasing) use M0's column unchanged, apart from their own configuration keys. The final stage (Section 4.8) also keeps every M0 setting, including 24 epochs, and only changes the training identities and the evaluation split.

4.7 Evaluation protocol¶

Development evaluation uses IR→RGB all-search, single-shot retrieval on the internal validation split (99 identities). Ten fixed gallery draws (seeds 0–9) are selected from the RGB candidate pool following the author's sampling procedure, and every model is scored on the same ten galleries. Cam2 gallery images are excluded for cam3 queries, following the SYSU protocol, and CMC is computed at identity level. Features are taken after the BN neck, L2-normalised and ranked by cosine similarity, without flip augmentation or re-ranking. We report mAP, mINP and Rank-k, averaged over the ten galleries. The evaluator was checked against hand-computed cases and against the author's evaluation code.

In this split, IR queries come only from camera 3 and RGB candidates only from cameras 4 and 5. Validation scores are therefore not comparable with published SYSU-MM01 test results.

Metrics. For each query the gallery is ranked by cosine similarity, with cam-2 images removed for cam-3 queries.

  • mAP: the mean over queries of the average precision over all correct gallery images.
  • mINP: the mean over queries of (number of correct images) / (rank of the last correct image), which shows how far down the hardest correct match lies.
  • CMC and Rank-k: identity-level, as in the SYSU protocol. A query's rank is the number of distinct identities ranked above its first correct image, and Rank-k is the share of queries whose first correct image comes within the top k identities.

Each metric is computed per gallery and averaged over the ten galleries; means and SDs over seeds are taken over these averages. Two models are compared on the same seed and gallery (30 pairs for three seeds), and we report the mean difference, the per-seed differences and the number of pairs in which one model is higher.

Robustness. Only the IR queries are perturbed; the gallery features are reused unchanged. There are nine fixed conditions: clean; a band filled with the ImageNet mean covering 10% or 20% of the image height at the top, middle or bottom; and Gaussian blur with σ = 1 or 2. Perturbations are deterministic and applied after resizing, before normalisation. Each run first re-extracts the clean features and checks them against the exported ones (src/robustness.py).

Test-time fusion (M2* only). As a separate variant outside the main protocol, M2*'s trained local features are concatenated with the global feature. The weights were fixed before the runs: the global feature takes half of the cosine similarity and the three regions share the rest. Fusion changes the retrieval dimension from 768 to 3,072.

Natural occlusion. Member A annotated 224 naturally occluded IR queries in the test split; the validation queries contain none. They are evaluated once, descriptively, on the final models only, and were never used for model selection.

Validation coverage. Validation IR queries come only from camera 3 and RGB candidates only from cameras 4 and 5, so validation scores serve internal comparisons only (see above). The test split covers all cameras and is evaluated in All-search and Indoor-search.

The core of sysu_metrics in src/evaluate.py (ranking, camera exclusion, identity-level CMC, AP and INP per query):

In [11]:
def sysu_metrics(distmat, q_ids, g_ids, q_cams, g_cams, max_rank=20):
    """SYSU evaluation; smaller distance = more similar. Returns identity-level CMC, mAP and mINP."""
    distmat = np.asarray(distmat, dtype=np.float64)
    q_ids, g_ids, q_cams, g_cams = map(np.asarray, (q_ids, g_ids, q_cams, g_cams))
    order = np.argsort(distmat, axis=1, kind="stable")
    cmc, aps, inps = np.zeros(max_rank), [], []
    for q in range(len(q_ids)):
        ranked = order[q]
        if q_cams[q] == 3:                              # cam3 queries ignore cam2 gallery images
            ranked = ranked[g_cams[ranked] != 2]
        ranked_ids = g_ids[ranked]
        hits = np.flatnonzero(ranked_ids == q_ids[q])
        if len(hits) == 0:                              # no correct image: excluded and counted
            continue
        identity_rank = len(np.unique(ranked_ids[:hits[0]]))   # distinct identities above the first hit
        if identity_rank < max_rank:
            cmc[identity_rank:] += 1
        aps.append(np.mean(np.arange(1, len(hits) + 1) / (hits + 1)))
        inps.append(len(hits) / (hits[-1] + 1))
    cmc /= len(aps)
    return {"cmc": cmc, "mAP": float(np.mean(aps)), "mINP": float(np.mean(inps)), "rank1": float(cmc[0])}

4.8 Final stage: 395 training identities and one test evaluation¶

After model selection on the validation split, the training and validation identities (296 + 99 = 395) were merged, and M0 and the selected model were retrained from the same ImageNet initialisation with seeds 17, 42 and 2026, then evaluated once on the 96 test identities. All other settings are as in development, including 24 epochs and the last checkpoint.

The selected model is M0 + CA. The local-supervision model M2* was the initial candidate; channel augmentation was added later with a selection rule fixed in advance (M0 + CA must exceed M0 in mean validation mAP, with the same sign on every seed), and it met this rule (Section 5.6).

def seed_stats(name, metric):
    values = 100 * np.array([run[metric] for run in val[name]])
    return values.mean(), (values.std(ddof=1) if len(values) > 1 else float("nan"))

def mean_sd(name, metric):
    mean, sd = seed_stats(name, metric)
    return f"{mean:.1f}" if np.isnan(sd) else f"{mean:.1f} ± {sd:.1f}"

baselines = ["V0", "M0", "AGW", "CAJ", "CAJ_fix"]

     mean_sd(n, "mAP"), mean_sd(n, "mINP"), mean_sd(n, "rank1"),
     *[f"{seed_stats(n, m)[0]:.1f}" for m in ("rank5", "rank10", "rank20")],
     resources[n]["params_m"], resources[n]["gflops"], resources[n]["gpu_hours"]]
    for n in baselines])

# Paired differences on the same galleries: 3 seeds × 10 galleries = 30 pairs (percentage points).
def paired(a, b, metric):
    return 100 * (np.array([r[f"g_{metric}"] for r in val[a]]) - np.array([r[f"g_{metric}"] for r in val[b]]))

rows = []
for a, b in (("V0", "M0"), ("AGW", "M0"), ("CAJ_fix", "M0"), ("CAJ_fix", "AGW")):
    for metric, label in (("mAP", "mAP"), ("rank1", "Rank-1")):
        diff = paired(a, b, metric)
        rows.append([f"{labels[a]} − {labels[b]}", label, f"{diff.mean() + 0.0:+.2f}",
                     " / ".join(f"{d:+.2f}" for d in diff.mean(axis=1)), f"{(diff > 0).sum()} / {diff.size}"])
show_table(["Comparison (A − B)", "Metric", "Mean", "Per seed (17 / 42 / 2026)", "Pairs where A is higher"], rows)

# Mean CMC curves (three seeds each).
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
for name in ("V0", "M0", "AGW", "CAJ_fix"):
    cmc = 100 * np.mean([run["cmc"] for run in val[name]], axis=0)
    ax.plot(range(1, 21), cmc, marker="o", ms=3, label=labels[name])
ax.set_xlabel("rank"); ax.set_ylabel("matching rate (%)"); ax.set_xticks([1, 5, 10, 15, 20])
ax.set_title("CMC on validation, mean of 3 seeds × 10 galleries"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
  • PMT components (M0 vs V0). M0 is 2.0 mAP and 4.1 Rank-1 points above V0 and higher on all 30 seed–gallery pairs, on every seed. The greyscale stage, MSEL and DCL therefore give a consistent gain over a plain ViT with the same backbone and schedule. mINP is level (24.4 vs 24.2), so the gain is in the first ranks rather than in the hardest matches.
  • Transformer PMT vs CNN baseline (M0 vs AGW). M0 is 3.9 mAP and 5.3 Rank-1 points above AGW on all 30 pairs, with about 3.6 times the parameters and computation. Backbone, input size, optimiser and losses all differ, so the gap cannot be attributed to the backbone alone.
  • Corrected CAJ vs M0. With seed 17 alone the two were level in mAP; over three seeds the corrected CAJ is 0.8 mAP below M0 (higher on 12 of 30 pairs) and level in Rank-1 (+0.02, 16 of 30). Its seed spread is the widest of the four valid baselines (Rank-1 SD 1.2), so the single-seed tie was partly chance. It reaches close to M0 with a ResNet-50 at about a quarter of the computation, but with 100 epochs and about 3.6 times M0's GPU time.
  • Corrected CAJ vs AGW. The corrected CAJ is 3.1 mAP and 5.3 Rank-1 points above AGW (29 of 30 pairs), in line with the published ordering. The gap combines channel augmentation, random erasing, the ADP loss, a larger batch, more epochs and the corrected weighting, so it is not the effect of channel augmentation alone; Section 5.6 isolates channel augmentation on PMT.
  • CAJ with the authors' code is about 20 points below AGW because of the training collapse described below.

5.3 CAJ training collapse and correction¶

With the authors' code, CAJ did not train stably on our split. The table shows per-epoch means for CAJ with the authors' code and with the corrected weighting, with AGW's training identity accuracy for reference.

50 0.01 0.219 0.976 0.013 0.996 1.000
81 0.001 0.169 0.984 0.010 0.997 1.000
100 0.001 0.158 0.984 0.010 0.997 —

For the first five epochs the ADP loss sat at its clamp value of 88, where its gradient is zero, so only the identity loss was learning. During epoch 6 the ADP term left the clamp and produced large gradients. By epoch 7, training identity accuracy had fallen from 0.85 to 0.03, close to chance (1/296). ADP settled near ln 2 ≈ 0.69, meaning the positive and negative distances had become equal: the features had collapsed. The model relearned the training identities (98% accuracy by epoch 100) but reached only 7.0% Rank-1 on validation.

The cause lies in the hard-sample weighting that AGW and CAJ share. When computing softmax weights over negatives, the code takes the maximum over a row that still contains masked-out zeros. With pre-BN features of norm about 50, every negative weight underflows, so the closest-negative distance evaluates to about 0. ADP then only pulls positives together, and nothing pushes different identities apart. AGW uses the same weighting, but its WRT loss has bounded gradients, and it trained normally. Taking the maximum over valid entries only restores real negative distances (about 26 at initialisation, instead of 0).

We retrained CAJ with only this change (masked_max in src/agw.py), reported as CAJfix; data, augmentation, losses, schedule and seed are unchanged. The ADP loss now starts at 1.65 rather than the clamp value and decreases steadily, training identity accuracy rises without a drop. The final model reaches 34.4% mAP and 33.1% Rank-1.

The weighting function from src/agw.py, with the upstream behaviour and our correction behind one flag:

In [19]:
def pairwise_distance(x):
    square = x.pow(2).sum(1, keepdim=True)
    return (square + square.t() - 2 * x @ x.t()).clamp(min=1e-12).sqrt()


def softmax_weights(dist, mask, masked_max=False):
    """Upstream takes the row max over dist * mask, so masked-out zeros join it; with large distances every
    negative weight then underflows and closest_negative is ~0. masked_max=True (CAJ_fix) uses valid entries only,
    and sets masked entries to -inf before exp so they cannot overflow."""
    if masked_max:
        valid = dist.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
        diff = valid - valid.max(dim=1, keepdim=True)[0]
    else:
        diff = dist - torch.max(dist * mask, dim=1, keepdim=True)[0]
    z = torch.sum(torch.exp(diff) * mask, dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6
    return torch.exp(diff) * mask / z


def weighted_extremes(features, labels, alpha=1.0, masked_max=False):
    """Softmax-weighted furthest positive / closest negative per anchor (self-match included, as upstream)."""
    dist = pairwise_distance(features)
    same = labels[:, None].eq(labels[None, :]).float()
    dist_ap, dist_an = dist * same, dist * (1 - same)
    furthest_positive = (dist_ap * softmax_weights(dist_ap * alpha, same, masked_max)).sum(1)
    closest_negative = (dist_an * softmax_weights(-dist_an * alpha, 1 - same, masked_max)).sum(1)
    return furthest_positive, closest_negative
In [20]:
# Pre-BN features with norm about 50, as in the collapsed run: the upstream weighting returns a closest-negative
# distance of about 0, so ADP sees no negatives; the corrected weighting returns the real distance.
torch.manual_seed(0)
features = F.normalize(torch.randn(64, 2048), dim=1) * 50
features_labels = torch.arange(16).repeat_interleave(4)
rows = []
for masked, name in ((False, "authors' code"), (True, "corrected (masked max)")):
    positive, negative = weighted_extremes(features, features_labels, masked_max=masked)
    rows.append([name, f"{positive.mean().item():.2f}", f"{negative.mean().item():.4f}"])
show_table(["Weighting", "Mean furthest-positive distance", "Mean closest-negative distance"], rows)

5.4 Smooth transition (S)¶

All results below are development validation measurements, averaged over the same ten galleries within each run. The ± values are sample standard deviations across training seeds. Statistics are recomputed from the embedded per-seed values. M1 and F values are transcribed at the precision published in docs/evaluation.md; rounding can change the final displayed SD digit (for example, M1 Rank-1 SD is 0.77 here versus 0.76 in the reported full-precision summary).

RQ1 result. M1 reaches 34.35 ± 0.56% mAP versus M0's 34.57 ± 0.46%. Its paired mAP differences are −0.29, −0.27 and −0.11 percentage points across seeds 17, 42 and 2026 (mean −0.22). Rank-1 is 31.86% versus 32.21%. Adding S to L also lowers mean mAP by 0.22 points (M3 versus M2). The tested schedule shows no retrieval benefit. Comparing the gap with seed SD is descriptive, not a significance or equivalence test.

Exposure control. On seed 17, F gives 34.39% mAP versus 34.38% for M0 and 34.09% for M1. F approximately matches M0 in this run; one seed cannot establish that exposure amount is irrelevant. Ten galleries are repeated evaluations of a trained model, not ten training replicates. F needs additional training seeds before a stronger schedule-versus-exposure conclusion is justified.

Interpretation and limits. PMT already has a grayscale stage and alignment losses. A taper may delay colour cues without introducing a new alignment objective; this is a hypothesis, not a mechanism established by retrieval scores. CAJfix's architecture and training differ from PMT, so its comparison cannot isolate channel augmentation; Section 5.6 provides the controlled M0 versus M0+CA comparison. Only the linear three-epoch window was tested. The figure in Section 4.3 plots the configured probabilities, not observed adaptation or M1/F training losses. Matched training trajectories would be required to test the adaptation explanation. S was not selected for final test-set evaluation.

Related configuration contribution. L3_B025 combines three local regions with β = 0.25 and disables S. Its seed-17 result (34.42% mAP, 31.94% Rank-1) is exploratory; the +0.04 mAP difference from M0 is not evidence of an improvement. The full q × β comparison appears in Section 5.5.

cond = extra["conditions"]
cond_short = ["clean", "top 10%", "top 20%", "mid 10%", "mid 20%", "bottom 10%", "bottom 20%", "blur σ=1", "blur σ=2"]
names = {"M0": "M0", "M2": "M2", "M2s": "M2*", "M3": "M3", "M0_BE": "M0 + BE", "M2s_BE": "M2* + BE",
         "M0_CA": "M0 + CA", "M2s_CA": "M2* + CA"}

def rob(name, seeds=None, source=None):
    """Array [seed, condition, gallery] of mAP in percent."""
    data = (source or extra["val_robustness"])[name]
    return 100 * np.array([[data[s][c] for c in cond] for s in (seeds or list(data))])

def rob_diff_rows(pairs, source=None, seeds=None):
    rows = []
    for a, b in pairs:
        diff = rob(a, seeds, source) - rob(b, seeds, source)
        rows.append([f"{names[a]} − {names[b]}"] + [f"{diff[:, i].mean():+.2f} ({(diff[:, i] > 0).sum()}/{diff[:, i].size})"
                                                     for i in range(len(cond))])
    return rows

show_table(["Model"] + cond_short,

  • Bottom occlusion is the hardest perturbation for every model. Covering the lowest 20% of the query reduces M0's mAP by 8.7 points, compared with 5.7 for the top 20% and 2.0 for the middle 20%. In these crops the legs and shoes appear to carry much of the identity information that survives the change of modality.
  • L gives no robustness gain. M2 and M2* stay within ±0.35 mAP of M0 under every condition. M2* keeps a small advantage only under middle occlusion (+0.30 and +0.33, higher on 20 and 18 of 30 pairs). On seed 17 alone M2* looked higher under every perturbation; over three seeds this does not hold.
  • S + L is below L. M3 is below M2 under all nine conditions (−0.1 to −0.5 mAP, higher on at most 9 of 30 pairs), so adding S to L does not help robustness either.

Fusion improves M2* under all nine conditions, but only by 0.06–0.26 mAP, while making the retrieval feature four times larger. The effect is consistent (26 of 27 seed–condition differences are positive) but too small to justify the cost, so every other result in this notebook retrieves with the global feature only.

Band erasing (negative result). In the tables above, band erasing lowers clean mAP by 0.89 for M0 (M0 + BE higher on only 6 of 30 pairs) and by 1.02 for M2*. Nor does it improve robustness: both BE models are lower than their counterparts under eight of nine conditions, and only bottom 20% occlusion is slightly higher (+0.17 and +0.21, about 20 of 30 pairs). A possible reason is that erasing a whole third of the image in half of the training samples removes information the model would otherwise learn from, while the test bands (10–20% of the height) are smaller. Band erasing was not used further.

M0 + CA is 1.45 mAP and 2.0 Rank-1 points above M0, higher on every seed (+1.47, +2.20, +0.67 mAP) and on 28 of 30 seed–gallery pairs. The gain is about three times M0's seed standard deviation (0.46 mAP) and holds across the CMC curve. M0 + CA is also 2.3 mAP above the corrected CAJ, so channel augmentation adds to PMT rather than only bringing PMT to the CNN's level. This satisfies the rule fixed before the result, and M0 + CA became the final candidate. No other configuration in Sections 5.4–5.5 met a comparable standard.

M2* + CA is below M0 + CA on every seed: −0.36 on seed 17 (evaluated by Member B) and −0.79 on seeds 42 and 2026 (higher on only 2 of 20 pairs), giving 35.4 ± 0.7 against 36.0 ± 0.4 mAP over three seeds. Member B's paired evaluation of all three seeds gives a mean difference of −0.66 (M2* + CA higher on only 6 of 30 pairs); the −0.64 implied by the table above differs only because two of its seeds come from our re-extracted features. It is also lower under all nine perturbations (−0.6 to −1.5). CA does help M2* itself (+0.75 on seeds 42 and 2026), so the two changes are compatible, but local supervision brings no further gain once CA is used, so the two gains are not additive. M0 + CA therefore remained the only candidate for the final stage.

5.7 Final test results¶

M0 and M0 + CA were retrained on the 395 training and validation identities with seeds 17, 42 and 2026 (24 epochs, about 0.7 GPU hours per run) and evaluated once on the 96 test identities.

Comparison with published results. SYSU-MM01 test set, single-shot, Rank-1 / mAP / mINP (%). Published numbers were checked against each paper; ours are means of three training seeds, each averaged over ten fixed galleries.

Method Backbone All-search Indoor-search
AGW, published [3] ResNet-50 47.50 / 47.65 / 35.30 54.17 / 62.97 / 59.23
CAJ, published [4] ResNet-50 69.88 / 66.89 / 53.61 76.26 / 80.37 / 76.79
PMT, published [1] ViT-B/16 67.53 / 64.98 / 51.86 71.66 / 76.52 / 72.74
Our M0 (PMT) ViT-B/16 66.3 / 64.6 / 51.8 71.5 / 76.8 / 73.2
Our M0 + CA ViT-B/16 68.2 / 66.2 / 53.2 73.3 / 78.4 / 74.8

What is comparable. PMT's published result uses the same dataset and test protocol as ours. Our M0 is within 0.4 mAP of it in All-search and slightly above it in Indoor-search mAP. The paper reports one trained model, while our numbers are means over three seeds, and the gap is well inside our seed SD (1.2 mAP for M0 in All-search).

What is not. The published AGW and CAJ results are listed for reference only. They come from the authors' own settings: a ResNet-50 at 288 × 144, their own schedules, and for CAJ the full method (channel augmentation together with channel erasing, greyscale augmentation and joint learning over original and augmented views). Published CAJ is above our M0 + CA, but the difference mixes all of these factors and cannot be attributed to any one of them. A fair comparison needs the same split, sampler and evaluator, so we retrained AGW and CAJ under ours (Section 5.2), where both are below M0. Our claim is therefore a controlled gain of channel augmentation over PMT, not a new state of the art.

With 395 identities each epoch has 695 batches instead of 633, so 24 epochs take 16,680 steps instead of 15,192. Training time is the sum of the per-batch times recorded in the training log, excluding data loading before the first step and feature export.

  • Indoor-search. The gain is +1.55 mAP and +1.76 Rank-1, with mAP higher on all 30 pairs. Indoor search uses only the indoor RGB cameras and has a higher baseline, and the gain is about the same size as in All-search.
  • Gain across ranks. The CMC curves differ most at the first ranks and almost meet by Rank-20 (98.5–99.4% for both models), so CA mainly moves the true match from the next few ranks to rank 1 (Section 5.8).

On the test set M0 + CA stays above M0 under all nine perturbations (+0.91 to +1.69 mAP, higher on 21–29 of 30 pairs). As on validation, its smallest gain is under top occlusion, where it is slightly lower on seed 17 (−0.17 and −0.41). The 224 naturally occluded queries, mostly people partly hidden by pillars or seen from the side, are 4.7 mAP harder than the rest for M0. CA improves them by +1.68, comparable to the gain on queries without occlusion (+1.59). The subset is small and was chosen by hand, so this is descriptive only: CA is a general improvement, not an occlusion-specific one.

5.8 Error analysis and retrieval examples¶

This section examines where the final models still fail. All statistics use the test set, All-search, three seeds × ten galleries (114,090 query–gallery cases per model).

In [31]:
err = extra["errors"]
bins = ["Rank 1", "Rank 2–3", "Rank 4–10", "Beyond 10"]
show_table(["Model"] + bins + ["Rank-1 errors with the true match in top 3", "… in top 10"],
           [[lab[m]] + [f"{100 * v:.1f}%" for v in err["models"][m]["bins"]]
            + [f"{100 * err['models'][m]['errors_in_top3']:.1f}%", f"{100 * err['models'][m]['errors_in_top10']:.1f}%"]
            for m in ("M0", "M0_CA")])
show_table(["Model", "Camera 3 mAP", "Camera 6 mAP", "Queries (cam 3 / cam 6)"],
           [[lab[m], f"{100 * np.mean(err['models'][m]['cam_mAP']['3']):.1f}", f"{100 * np.mean(err['models'][m]['cam_mAP']['6']):.1f}",
             "{} / {}".format(err["models"][m]["cam_queries"]["3"], err["models"][m]["cam_queries"]["6"])] for m in ("M0", "M0_CA")])
p = err["paired"]
show_table(["Rank-1, same query, seed and gallery", "Share of cases"],
           [["M0 wrong → M0 + CA right", f"{100 * p['fixed'] / p['total']:.1f}%"],
            ["M0 right → M0 + CA wrong", f"{100 * p['broken'] / p['total']:.1f}%"],
            ["Net change", f"{100 * (p['fixed'] - p['broken']) / p['total']:+.1f} points"]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 1.8))
colours = ["#0B5C80", "#3E95BD", "#9BCBE0", "#C9D1D7"]
for y, m in enumerate(("M0_CA", "M0")):
    left = 0
    for v, c, b in zip(err["models"][m]["bins"], colours, bins):
        ax.barh(y, 100 * v, left=left, color=c, edgecolor="white", label=b if y == 0 else None)
        ax.text(left + 50 * v, y, f"{100 * v:.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,
                color="white" if c in colours[:2] else "black")
        left += 100 * v
ax.set_yticks([0, 1], [lab["M0_CA"], lab["M0"]]); ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_xlabel("% of test queries: rank of the true match")
ax.legend(ncol=4, fontsize=8, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), frameon=False)

Net change +1.9 points
  • Most errors are near misses. M0 + CA ranks the true match first for 68.2% of query–gallery cases and second or third for another 15.5%; only 5.7% are outside the top 10. Of its Rank-1 errors, 48.8% have the true match in the top 3 and 82.1% in the top 10. Compared with M0, CA moves cases from rank 4 and beyond to rank 1, while the share at ranks 2–3 stays the same.
  • Camera 6 is harder. Queries from IR camera 6 reach 63.6 mAP against 68.8 for camera 3 (M0 + CA). CA improves results on both cameras (+1.9 and +1.3).
  • CA changes many individual results. For the same query, seed and gallery, CA turns 9.1% of cases from wrong to right at Rank-1 and 7.2% from right to wrong. The net gain of 1.9 points is the difference of two much larger movements, so CA re-ranks many queries rather than only fixing the hardest ones.

Retrieval examples. For M0 + CA (seed 17, gallery 0), six queries were drawn at random (sample seed 0) from those whose true match is at rank 2–3 (near, n = 570 of 3,803) and six from those whose true match is outside the top 5 (miss, n = 417), with scripts/retrieval_cases.py. Four of the twelve are shown, one per failure type: the IR query on the left, then the top three gallery images; green = same person, red = different person.

The sampled cases illustrate four failure types:

  • (a) Similar build and clothing cut. The top-ranked person has the same silhouette and clothing shape, which IR cannot separate without colour.
  • (b) Low-contrast camera-6 image. The query is dark and blurred, and the correct image is a near tie with the top result.
  • (c) Bright IR clothing. A shirt that is bright in IR can be almost any colour in RGB, so a different person in light clothing ranks first.
  • (d) Back view. A backpack covers much of the body and dominates the feature.

These cases form a small random sample, and the failure types reflect our visual inspection rather than a measured distribution.

6. Discussion¶

6.1 Baselines and channel augmentation¶

PMT's components give a small but consistent gain: over three seeds M0 is above the plain ViT (V0) on all 30 seed–gallery pairs, and above the CNN baseline AGW by about 4 mAP points at roughly 3.6 times the computation. The corrected CAJ comes close to M0 with a ResNet-50 but is 0.8 mAP lower over three seeds; its single-seed tie with M0 did not hold, which is why every comparison in this notebook uses three seeds.

Channel augmentation is the one change that clearly improves PMT on validation (+1.45 mAP, all seeds). PMT already narrows the modality gap with a greyscale stage; copying a single colour channel to all three keeps varying the colour statistics throughout training, which appears to be a stronger version of the same idea. This also bears on RQ1: a smoother greyscale schedule did not help (Section 5.4), while stronger, persistent colour perturbation did.

The CAJ run shows that published code can be numerically fragile outside its original setting. A masking detail that is harmless for AGW's loss made CAJ's loss collapse the features, and only the training curve and a pilot evaluation exposed it. Correcting that one detail raised CAJ from 7.0% to 33.1% Rank-1 (seed 17). We therefore evaluated a short pilot before every full run and inspected each loss term rather than the total alone.

6.2 Answers to the research questions¶

RQ1: smooth transition. The tested three-epoch linear schedule does not improve retrieval: M1 is below M0 in mAP on all three training seeds, by 0.22 percentage points on average. F approximately matches M0 on seed 17, but its single run does not settle the effect of exposure amount. No gain was observed from adding S to L either (Section 5.4).

RQ2: local identity supervision. Regional identity supervision keeps retrieval performance close to M0 across three seeds (Section 5.5).

RQ3: combining S and L. Adding S to L provides no additional retrieval benefit.

RQ4: channel augmentation. CA is the only change that clearly improves PMT: +1.45 mAP on validation (every seed, 28 of 30 pairs), and on the test set, evaluated once, +1.6 mAP in All-search and +1.55 in Indoor-search. The gain holds under all nine perturbations and on naturally occluded queries, and it adds no test-time cost. A likely reason is that copying one channel removes colour cues, which IR images lack, throughout training, whereas PMT's grey stage does so only for six epochs. We have not tested this, for example with attention maps.

Negative results. Three further changes did not help, and we report them as results. Band erasing costs about 1 mAP and does not improve robustness (Section 5.5). Combining L with CA is 0.66 mAP below CA alone, so the gains are not additive (Section 5.6). Test-time fusion of local features adds at most 0.26 mAP at four times the feature size (Section 5.5). Single-seed differences of up to 0.6 mAP (M2* +0.5 and M2 −0.6 on seed 17) disappeared over three seeds; M0 itself varies by 0.5 mAP across seeds.

Failure types. The remaining errors are mostly near misses (49% of Rank-1 errors have the true match in the top 3). They come from people of similar build and clothing cut, low-contrast camera-6 images, bright IR clothing whose colour cannot be inferred, and back views dominated by a backpack (Section 5.8).

6.3 Limitations¶

  • One dataset and one setting. All results come from SYSU-MM01, IR → RGB, single-shot. We did not test RGB → IR, multi-shot or other datasets (RegDB, LLCM).
  • Comparison with published results. Training identities, camera coverage (on validation, cam-3 queries against cam-4/5 galleries only) and training details differ from published settings. Only PMT's published test result is directly comparable; published AGW and CAJ scores are listed for reference only.
  • Seed noise. Three training seeds resolve differences of about 0.5 mAP at best (M0's seed SD is 0.46 mAP on validation and 1.2 on test). "No gain" for S and L means no gain we can detect.
  • Limited tuning. CA's probability (0.5) follows CAJ and was not tuned; L was tuned on a small q × β grid with one seed.
  • Order of experiments. CA was chosen after the S and L study and after the configuration freeze (Section 4.8). Its decision rule was written before its runs, and the test set was used once.
  • Robustness. Synthetic bands and blur are a controlled stress test, not real occlusion; the natural-occlusion subset (224 queries) is small and selected by hand.
  • Explanation. That CA works by reducing reliance on colour is a hypothesis we have not tested.
  • Absolute performance. At 66% test mAP no model here is ready for real-world deployment; the results support design choices, not operational reliability.

6.4 Follow-up work and conclusion¶

Follow-up work.

  • Test CA on RegDB and LLCM, and in RGB → IR and multi-shot settings.
  • Compare attention maps of M0 and M0 + CA to test whether CA reduces reliance on colour.
  • Target the remaining failure types: low-contrast camera-6 images and back views.
  • Tune CA's probability, and test the full CAJ joint-learning setup on PMT.

Conclusion. We re-implemented PMT and three baselines under one verified evaluation protocol, with fixed galleries and three training seeds, and tested three training-time extensions with controls. A smooth grey-to-colour schedule (S) and local identity supervision (L) do not improve PMT, alone or together, and their single-seed gains did not replicate; band erasing and test-time fusion did not help either. CAJ's channel augmentation, adapted to PMT's batch structure, improves PMT on validation (+1.45 mAP) and on the official test set (+1.6 mAP in All-search, +1.55 in Indoor-search), on every seed, under perturbation and on naturally occluded queries, at no test-time cost.

Appendix A. Code and reproduction¶

The complete code (data interface, models, losses, training, feature export, evaluation and robustness tools), all run configurations and the tests are in project_code.zip, submitted together with this notebook. The core of each method is shown next to its description in Section 4. Datasets, checkpoints and exported features are not included.

Path Contents
src/ data and sampler, PMT model and losses, S schedule, local head, AGW/CAJ, training, feature export, evaluator, robustness
configs/ base.json plus one file per experiment; every run is the base merged with one experiment file
scripts/ data and pretrained-weight preparation, cluster job scripts, fusion and natural-occlusion evaluation
README.md, ATTRIBUTION.md setup notes; sources, pinned upstream commits and our changes to third-party code
tests/ unit tests, incl. numerical checks against the authors' code and the leakage rules

Every model name in this notebook corresponds to one configuration file in configs/experiments/ (the --experiment argument), trained with seeds 17, 42 and 2026:

Reproduction (Linux, one NVIDIA GPU; about 0.8 h per PMT run on an L40S):

pip install -r requirements-katana-lock.txt
python scripts/prepare_pretrained.py && python scripts/prepare_data.py
python -m src.train --experiment M0 --run-id dev_M0_seed17 --seed 17 --device cuda
python -m src.export_features --checkpoint checkpoints/dev_M0_seed17/last.pt --split val --modality ir  --output artifacts/results/dev_M0_seed17/query_val.npz
python -m src.export_features --checkpoint checkpoints/dev_M0_seed17/last.pt --split val --modality rgb --output artifacts/results/dev_M0_seed17/gallery_pool_val.npz
python -m src.evaluate run --query artifacts/results/dev_M0_seed17/query_val.npz --gallery-pool artifacts/results/dev_M0_seed17/gallery_pool_val.npz --output-dir artifacts/results/dev_M0_seed17/eval_all

AGW and CAJ use python -m src.train_agw --experiment AGW|CAJ|CAJ_fix. Final-stage checkpoints export the test split instead of validation.
